safetyNote: This app treats Lactifluus piperatus as unsuitable for casual eating because its latex is intensely peppery and white milkcaps have close lookalikes. The DGfM does list it as edible only with the instruction to fry thoroughly; this is not a recommendation to taste or eat a specimen identified from a picture. Never eat it raw. Have any intended food collection identified by a local expert, and follow the regional preparation advice.

sections.title: Large dry white funnel
sections.text: The substantial cap is often about 6–16 cm wide, cream-white with a dry, finely matte, nearly smooth surface. Its margin begins rolled inward and the centre becomes markedly depressed or funnel-shaped. Age and handling can leave buff or tan patches. The thick, brittle flesh remains white in section, and the pale stem is firm, fairly stout and smooth to finely bloomed; older stems can become hollow.

sections.title: Exceptionally crowded gills and white latex
sections.text: Very narrow, exceptionally close white to cream gills extend down the stem. Breaking a gill brings out white latex with an intensely hot or peppery character. Do not taste an unidentified mushroom to test this. Published descriptions differ on whether the dried milk develops greenish tones, and molecular studies show that this change cannot reliably separate L. piperatus from the near-twin L. glaucescens. The spore deposit is white.

sections.title: Woodland and lookalikes
sections.text: It is an ectomycorrhizal woodland fungus, often recorded with deciduous trees including beech, fruiting from summer into autumn. L. vellereus has a more woolly cap and more widely spaced gills; L. glaucescens can be almost identical in the field and may need microscopic examination of the cap surface. Russula delica can look like a large white milkcap but does not exude latex. The cap, tightly packed gills and a fresh cut must all be inspected.

sections.title: Food guidance is not uniform
sections.text: The German Society for Mycology includes L. piperatus on its positive edible list with the explicit condition 'fry thoroughly'. The Missouri Department of Conservation also calls it edible but too peppery for most people, while other European guides find it unsuitable on taste grounds. These differences should not be flattened into a claim that the species is universally poisonous or universally suitable. The app's inedible flag is a practical caution, and a picture cannot establish species-level identity within this group.

traits: Large dry, matte cream-white cap, often 6–16 cm, becoming deeply depressed or funnel-shaped
Exceptionally crowded, very narrow white to cream decurrent gills
Stout white smooth stem; thick brittle white flesh; older stems may hollow
White latex with strongly peppery character; its later greenish change is unreliable for separation from L. glaucescens
White spore deposit; woodland association with broadleaf trees including beech
Close white milkcap lookalikes may need microscopy for confirmation
